newsitem.title: UK: UK output data suggest further rate cuts unlikely.
newsitem.headline: UK output data suggest further rate cuts unlikely.

text.p: Strong UK July industrial production data suggest interest rates may have bottomed at 5.75 percent, although the pickup in demand remains tentative and firms are still grappling with a stocks overhang.
"I think we should see it as a bounce-back from a weak June rather than necessarily the start of a better trend," said John Shepperd, chief economist at Yamaichi international Europe.
"But I think rates have bottomed. I think the economy is going to accelerate pretty well from now on in and we will see GDP on a quarterly basis above rather than below trend."

Industrial production was up 0.5 percent in July and 0.9 percent year-on-year, while manufacturing output rose 0.5 percent in the month and 0.3 percent year-on-year. Andrew Snowball of Cooperative Bank said Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke is likely to have seen the data before Wednesday's monetary meeting, which left rates unchanged.

"I think there is almost no chance of another cut," he told Reuters Financial Television. "The economy will gradually gain strength in the months ahead. But by the same token I don't expect Clarke to put rates higher in spite of his rhetoric before the election."
However, Shepperd doubts that the output data had an impact on Clarke's decision.

"I think the reason he didn't move was the perception that the economy is picking up steam, driven by the consumer sector, that growth will soon be above-trend and that there are doubts about the inflation target on a longer-term view," he said.
Ian Shepherdson of HSBC Markets said the figures were the first extremely modest sign of an upturn after three months in which output had been flat or fallen.
Capital goods performed much better than consumer goods due to strong export demand, he noted.
"On the other hand, even after a small upward revisio to June, output in the three months to July was flat compared to the previous three months," Shepherdson said.
"Demand is certainly recovering, but the stock overhang is still enormous and many firms can meet new orders simply by reaching for the shelves rather than increasing production."
Shepherdson sees output growth recovering to an annual rate of around 2.0 percent in the next few months.
"Hardly a boom, and not even fast enough to prevent further job losses," he said. "Mr Clarke won't see these figures as an obstacle to a further rate cut before Christmas."
Kevin Adams of BZW said it was very difficult to conceive of circumstances in which the Chancellor could make a convincing case for reducing rates further, but he did not completely rule one out.

"As we go into the autumn, with the party conferences and the budget in particular -- where Clarke will obviously be quite constrained in terms of what he can do -- that may be the time when he chooses to slip in a further cut," he told RFTV.
"But I would say there is a very low chance at the moment." Andrew Cates of UBS said today's figures suggested manufacturing was beginning to turn the corner.
He noted that inflation and retail sales data would form the backdrop to the next monetary meeting on September 23.
"Activity in most sectors of the economy now seems to be picking up, including one of this year's worst performers, the manufacturing sector," he said.

"As such, although Clarke would clearly love to reduce base rates again, ous best guess is that the current strength of the eocnomy will force him to stay his hand and he will probably leave rates on hold for the foreseeable future."
